A game that came for free

Built by Cinematronics and published by Maxis as part of Full Tilt! Pinball. One of its tables, Space Cadet, was licensed to Microsoft.

1995

Plus! 95

Add-on pack, sold separately

1996

NT 4.0

Now bundled with Windows

2000

2000 & Me

Shipped in both

2001

XP

32-bit only. The 64-bit edition shipped without it

2007

Vista

Gone

Sources: Wikipedia (Full Tilt! Pinball); BetaWiki; Raymond Chen, The Old New Thing

Then 64-bit broke the physics

01

In the 64-bit build, collision detection stopped working.

10

The ball passed through objects, sometimes falling through the plunger instead of launching.

11

The code came from another company and had almost no documentation.

Result

Removed

Raymond Chen and a colleague couldn’t find a fix in reasonable time. Vista shipped without Pinball.

Sources: Raymond Chen (The Old New Thing); PCWorld, Aug 2026; VirtuallyFun, Jun 2026

Microsoft had the source code. And still gave up.

The bottleneck was never access to the code. It was understanding it.

Reverse Engineer Anything

Why every app you ship is becoming open source.

Ibis Prevedello · Pocket · October 23, 2026

Reverse engineering isn’t new

IDA Pro

The industry standard since the 1990s

Ghidra

Built inside the NSA, open-sourced in 2019

Hopper

The go-to for macOS and iOS binaries

2021

The community decompiled Space Cadet from the original .exe and ported it to Linux, macOS, Android and the browser.

It worked. But it took an expert and a lot of manual work.

If you ship the binary, you ship the code

Rebuilding an app from its binary is becoming trivial. That leaves three paths:

01

Web app

The code stays on the server. Nobody downloads the binary.

10

Open source

Open it yourself, before someone else does.

11

Closed source

Gets a parallel open version, rebuilt through reverse engineering.

What this changes

Already happening

  • Free clones of paid software are already appearing.
  • Niche forks: take a closed app and evolve it for a different audience.
  • Chamath on All-In: “All software IPs are now rendered worthless.”

Counterpoints

  • Reading a binary, rebuilding an app and winning users are three different things.
  • Studios are answering with takedowns: Activision, Bethesda.
  • Indie devs fear copies of their games and apps.

Does shipping closed-source software still make sense?

Sources: Corporate Waters (Substack); Medium; InfoQ; Decrypt, Oct 2026
